title: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary · Units 15–16 (reviewed)
description: Reviewed vocabulary on school subjects, classroom objects, education, letters, email, internet, telephones, text messages and polite telephone conversations. Includes original practice sentences and British English IPA.
sourceNotice: Learning targets have been checked against the source teaching pages, illustrations and exercises. Explanations and practice examples were written for VocabLab. The book's illustrations and full exercises are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Unit 15: teaching sections A–C, labelled classroom illustrations, common mistake on homework, and Exercises 15.1–15.5. Unit 16: teaching sections A–D, labelled communication illustrations, telephone dialogue, tip, and Exercises 16.1–16.5.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British English IPA is provided as learning support. Connected speech and regional pronunciations may vary. Independent item-by-item phonetic validation and browser audio testing are not claimed.
audit.cannotGuarantee: The library entries are not a replacement for the book illustrations or complete exercise activities. Browser microphone, text-to-speech and speech-recognition behaviour require separate testing.
audit.languagePolicy: English throughout; only pt fields contain Portuguese translations.

units.title: Unit 15 — At school and university
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary, 3rd edition, Unit 15, printed pages 36–37 (PDF pages 37–38); original practice examples.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.example: History is my favourite subject.
items.note: At school, a subject is an area of study, such as history or maths. It can also mean a topic in other contexts.

items.example: We have English lessons on Tuesdays.
items.note: Names of languages begin with a capital letter in English: English, French and Spanish.

items.example: My cousin enjoys maths at school.
items.note: Maths is the usual British English shortened form of mathematics; American English commonly uses math.

items.example: We studied ancient Egypt in history today.
items.note: History is the study of events in the past. At school it is usually an uncountable subject name.

items.example: In geography, we learn about different countries.
items.note: Geography is the study of countries, places and the physical world. Do not confuse it with geometry.

items.example: My biology class starts at nine.
items.note: Biology is the study of living things, including plants and animals.

items.example: We draw and paint in art lessons.
items.note: In a school timetable, art names the subject in which students may draw or paint.

items.example: She studies French and Spanish in modern languages.
items.note: Modern languages refers to living languages taught at school, such as French and Spanish.

items.example: We play basketball in PE.
items.note: PE stands for physical education. Pronounce the two letters separately.

items.example: Our physical education teacher organises games.
items.note: Physical education is the full form of PE, a school subject involving exercise and sport.

items.example: Students use computers in ICT lessons.
items.note: ICT stands for information communication technology in the source material. Pronounce the letters separately.

items.example: Information communication technology is part of our timetable.
items.note: The source expands ICT as information communication technology. Information and communication technology is also common.

items.example: We learn about different substances in chemistry.
items.note: Chemistry is the study of substances and how they react or change.

items.example: Physics is difficult for some students.
items.note: Physics is the name of a school subject. Although it ends in -s, it usually takes a singular verb: Physics is interesting.

items.example: She sings in her music lesson.
items.note: Music is generally uncountable when referring to music in general: listen to music, not listen to a music.

items.example: The teacher wrote the date on the board.
items.note: A classroom board is a surface used for writing or drawing; whiteboard names a particular kind of board.

items.example: The school put the timetable on the noticeboard.
items.note: A noticeboard is a board for displaying announcements or information, not for writing a lesson on.

items.pt: folha de papel; pedaço de papel
items.example: Could you give me a piece of paper, please?
items.note: Paper is usually uncountable as a material. Say a piece of paper or two pieces of paper when counting.

items.example: I drew a map with a pencil.
items.note: A pencil is used for writing or drawing and can usually be erased. Compare pen.

items.example: I write new words in my notebook.
items.note: At school, a notebook is a book of blank or lined pages for writing notes. Compare textbook and laptop.

items.example: Our geography textbook has many maps.
items.note: A textbook is a book used to study a subject. A notebook is generally used for taking notes.

items.example: I need a rubber to correct my drawing.
items.note: In British English, a rubber removes pencil marks from paper. American English usually calls it an eraser.

items.example: We used a drawing pin to put up the notice.
items.note: In British English, a drawing pin holds paper to a noticeboard; thumbtack is common in American English.

items.example: The teacher used an OHP for the diagrams.
items.note: OHP stands for overhead projector. Pronounce each letter separately; it is an older classroom device.

items.example: The picture appeared on the screen from the overhead projector.
items.note: An overhead projector projects material onto a screen or wall. OHP is its abbreviation.

items.example: Please use the board rubber before the next lesson.
items.note: A board rubber wipes writing off a classroom board. Compare the smaller rubber used on paper.

items.example: Use a blue board pen on the whiteboard.
items.note: A board pen is a pen for writing on a classroom board, especially a whiteboard; whiteboard marker is also common.

items.example: I filled in the form with a black pen.
items.note: A pen writes with ink. Compare a pencil, which can usually be erased.

items.example: My pencil sharpener is in my bag.
items.note: A pencil sharpener makes the point of a pencil sharp again.

items.pt: carteira; mesa de estudo ou trabalho
items.example: She left her textbook on the desk.
items.note: A desk is a table used for working or studying, for example in a classroom or office.

items.example: There is a whiteboard near the door.
items.note: A whiteboard is a smooth, usually white writing surface. Use a suitable board marker rather than chalk.

items.example: Our teacher uses a computer in class.
items.note: A computer can help students study or work. The word also appears in the next unit about communication.

items.example: The school has a DVD player in the language room.
items.note: A DVD player plays video discs. DVD is pronounced as separate letters.

items.example: Use a ruler to draw a straight line.
items.note: A ruler is used for measuring lengths and drawing straight lines.

items.example: Our science teacher is very patient.
items.note: A teacher is a person who teaches. A teacher teaches a subject to students.

items.example: My sister teaches English to children.
items.note: Teach means give instruction to someone. The past and past participle are both taught: teach–taught–taught.

items.example: The students are studying for their exams.
items.note: A student is a person who studies. In the source, children go to school and students go to university.

items.example: I study maths every afternoon.
items.note: Study means spend time learning a subject. Compare teach, which describes what a teacher does.

items.pt: ir à escola; frequentar a escola
items.example: My brother goes to school near our house.
items.note: Say go to school without the when you mean attend school as a student.

items.pt: ir para a universidade; frequentar a universidade
items.example: She hopes to go to university next year.
items.note: In British English, go to university usually has no article when it means study at a university.

items.example: We learn new expressions every week.
items.note: Learn means gain knowledge or a skill. Both learnt and learned are accepted past forms in British English.

items.example: Children learn to read at school.
items.note: Use learn to + base verb for acquiring a skill: learn to read, learn to swim.

items.example: My son is learning to write short sentences.
items.note: Use learn to + base verb for acquiring a skill: learn to write.

items.example: I'm doing a short English course.
items.note: A course is a programme or series of lessons on a particular subject.

items.example: I want to do an evening course in French.
items.note: The source uses do a course to mean take part in a course. Do not say make a course in this meaning.

items.example: Our final exam is on Thursday.
items.note: Exam is a short form of examination. You can take an exam, pass an exam or fail an exam.

items.pt: fazer uma prova; prestar um exame
items.example: I'll take my driving exam next month.
items.note: Take an exam means sit an examination; it does not mean you passed it.

items.example: We did a difficult English exam yesterday.
items.note: The source gives do an exam as an alternative to take an exam in British English.

items.example: My friend studied hard and passed the exam.
items.note: Pass an exam means achieve a satisfactory result. Compare take an exam and fail an exam.

items.example: He was disappointed because he failed the exam.
items.note: Fail an exam means not achieve the required result. It is the opposite of pass an exam.

items.example: My final exam is at the end of June.
items.note: A final exam is an examination at the end of a course or study period.

items.example: She has a degree in chemistry.
items.note: A degree is a qualification awarded by a university after completing a programme of study.

items.example: He wants to get a degree in biology.
items.note: Get a degree means earn a university qualification after completing the required studies.

items.example: My homework takes about an hour.
items.note: Homework is uncountable: say some homework or a lot of homework, not homeworks.

items.example: We usually do our homework after dinner.
items.note: The source explicitly teaches do homework, not make homework or do homeworks.

items.example: My maths teacher gives us a quiz on Fridays.
items.note: Use a subject name before teacher to identify what someone teaches: a maths teacher.

items.example: Mr Wilson teaches maths at our school.
items.note: Teachers teach maths; students study maths. Teach usually refers to giving instruction.

items.example: She studies maths at university.
items.note: Students study maths to learn the subject. Compare teach maths.

items.example: She does well at school because she studies regularly.
items.note: Do well at school means achieve good results in schoolwork. This phrase occurs in Exercise 15.4.

items.example: Art was my favourite subject at school.
items.note: Favourite subject means the school subject you like most. Favourite is the British English spelling; favorite is American.

learningObjectives: Identify core school subjects, including maths, PE and ICT, and explain the abbreviations PE and ICT.
Name classroom objects and distinguish a notebook, a textbook, a board and a noticeboard.
Distinguish teach, study and learn in educational contexts.
Use do a course, take or do an exam, pass or fail an exam and get a degree correctly.
Use go to school and go to university to describe attendance at educational institutions.
Use do homework correctly and recognise that homework is uncountable.
Talk about favourite subjects and performance at school.

units.title: Unit 16 — Communications
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary, 3rd edition, Unit 16, printed pages 38–39 (PDF pages 39–40); original practice examples.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.example: I wrote a letter to my grandmother.
items.note: A letter is a written message, usually on paper, sent to someone. Compare email.

items.example: Please write your address clearly on the envelope.
items.note: In this unit, address is a noun meaning the details needed to send something to a person or place.

items.example: I bought two stamps at the post office.
items.note: A stamp is attached to an envelope or package to show that postage has been paid.

items.example: Her name is on the envelope.
items.note: An envelope is a paper cover used to hold a letter. Put the letter in the envelope.

items.example: Don't forget to write the date at the top.
items.note: Here, date means the day, month and year written on a letter or other document.

items.pt: caixa de correio; caixa postal de postagem
items.example: There is a red letter box near the station.
items.note: The illustration shows a public British letter box for posting letters; a letterbox can also mean a slot in a door.

items.word: put a stamp on an envelope
items.example: You need to put a stamp on the envelope first.
items.note: Use on with the envelope: put a stamp on an envelope. The stamp goes on the outside.

items.example: Can you post this letter for me tomorrow?
items.note: Post a letter means send it by mail in British English. Mail a letter is also common, especially in American English.

items.example: I write a letter to my aunt every month.
items.note: Write a letter is a natural verb–noun combination. It is practised in Exercise 16.5.

items.example: I use my computer to send emails.
items.note: A computer can be used to write and send emails or search the internet.

items.example: The email is open on the screen.
items.note: The screen shows pictures or text on a computer or other electronic device.

items.example: This keyboard has black keys.
items.note: A keyboard has keys used to type letters, numbers and other characters.

items.example: I clicked the link with my mouse.
items.note: A computer mouse moves the pointer on the screen. In another meaning, the animal has the irregular plural mice.

items.example: He takes his laptop to university.
items.note: A laptop is a portable computer. Compare notebook in Unit 15, meaning a book for writing notes.

items.example: I saved my homework on a memory stick.
items.note: A memory stick is a small portable device used to store electronic files; USB stick is also common.

items.example: I got an email from my teacher.
items.note: Email can be a noun or a verb: an email, send an email, email someone.

items.example: I got an email about the new course.
items.note: Get an email means receive an email. It does not mean write or send one.

items.example: Could you send me an email with the details?
items.note: Send an email means transmit a message electronically. Compare get an email.

items.example: Be careful when you share information online.
items.note: Online can be an adjective or adverb. Say go online or share information online, not in online.

items.example: I used a search engine to find a language dictionary.
items.note: A search engine is an online service for finding information; the phrase appears in the unit tip.

items.example: I go online after work to read the news.
items.note: Go online means connect to or use the internet. The phrase occurs in Exercise 16.5.

items.example: You should check information before sharing it.
items.note: Information is uncountable: say some information or a piece of information, not informations.

items.example: What is your email address?
items.note: An email address includes a name, an @ sign, and a domain. Read @ as at and . as dot.

items.example: Read the @ sign as at in an email address.
items.note: In an email address, the symbol @ is pronounced at.

items.example: Say dot when you read the full stop in an email address.
items.note: In email or website addresses, the full stop symbol (.) is read as dot.

items.example: A tablet is a useful mobile device.
items.note: A mobile device is a portable electronic device, such as a phone or tablet.

items.example: I've left my mobile at home.
items.note: In British English, mobile is a common short form of mobile phone.

items.example: There's a telephone on the office desk.
items.note: Telephone is a more formal or longer word for phone; it can also be used as a verb.

items.example: There is an old phone box in the village.
items.note: A phone box is a small public place or booth with a telephone, traditionally common in Britain.

items.example: I got a phone call from my uncle.
items.note: Phone call is a countable noun: make a phone call or get a phone call.

items.example: I need to make a phone call before lunch.
items.note: Use make a phone call, not do a phone call.

items.example: I'll phone my sister tonight.
items.note: Phone can be a transitive verb: phone someone, not phone to someone.

items.example: Her smartphone is in her bag.
items.note: A smartphone is a mobile phone that can run apps and access the internet.

items.example: Remember to take your phone with you.
items.note: Take something with you means bring it when you go somewhere. Take your phone with you is a useful pattern.

items.example: Please turn off your phone during the exam.
items.note: Turn off is separable: turn off your phone or turn your phone off. With it, say turn it off.

items.example: Could I have your phone number?
items.note: A phone number is the sequence of digits used to call someone.

items.example: My mobile number has changed.
items.note: A mobile number is the telephone number associated with a mobile phone.

items.example: Can you answer the phone, please?
items.note: Answer the phone means respond when the telephone rings.

items.pt: deixar uma mensagem na caixa postal
items.example: If she doesn't answer, I'll leave a voicemail.
items.note: Leave a voicemail means record a spoken message when a person does not answer.

items.pt: mandar mensagem de texto para alguém
items.example: I'll text you when I get home.
items.note: Text can be a verb: text someone, not text to someone. It means send a text message.

items.pt: enviar uma mensagem de texto a alguém
items.example: He sent his mother a text message.
items.note: You can say send someone a text message or send a text message to someone.

items.example: I got a text message this morning.
items.note: A text message is a written message sent by phone. You can send or receive one.

items.pt: ler um número de telefone em voz alta
items.example: Please read out your phone number slowly.
items.note: Read out a phone number means say its digits aloud. This skill is practised in Exercise 16.4.

items.example: My number starts with 'oh seven'.
items.note: In British English, the digit 0 in a phone number can be said as oh. Zero is also possible.

items.pt: duplo; duas ocorrências do mesmo número
items.example: In a phone number, you can say 'double three' for 33.
items.note: When two identical digits are together in a phone number, double may replace saying the digit twice: double six.

items.example: Hello! Is this the library?
items.note: Hello is a common greeting when answering a telephone or starting a conversation.

items.example: Hello, it's Maria here. May I speak to Tom?
items.note: This is a natural spoken example of It's [name] here. Replace Maria with a suitable name.

items.word: Can I speak to Daniel, please?
items.pt: Posso falar com Daniel, por favor?
items.example: Can I speak to Daniel, please? He's in the office today.
items.note: Can I speak to [name], please? is a polite way to ask for someone on the phone.

items.example: I'm sorry, but she's in a meeting.
items.note: I'm sorry is a polite expression for giving unwelcome information or apologising.

items.example: I'm afraid he's not here at the moment.
items.note: At the moment means now or currently. Say he is not here at the moment.

items.example: She's busy now. Can I take a message?
items.note: Can I take a message? offers to note what the caller wants to tell someone else.

items.example: There is a message for you on the desk.
items.note: A message can be information sent digitally or a note left for someone who cannot answer a call.

items.word: Could you tell him I called?
items.pt: Você poderia dizer a ele que liguei?
items.example: Could you tell him I called this morning?
items.note: Could you tell him I called? is a polite request. Tell normally takes a person directly: tell him.

items.example: I'll call back later when she is free.
items.note: Call back means phone again or return a call. Later means at a subsequent time.

items.example: Goodbye, and thank you for calling.
items.note: Goodbye is a standard way to end a conversation or telephone call.

items.example: OK, see you tomorrow. Bye!
items.note: Bye is a shorter and more informal way to say goodbye.

items.example: I prefer to text my friends in the evening.
items.note: Use prefer to + verb to talk about a preferred activity: I prefer to text my friends.

learningObjectives: Name the main parts of a letter and describe putting a stamp on an envelope and posting a letter.
Identify common computer equipment and basic internet communication vocabulary.
Ask for and read out email addresses, using at for @ and dot for a full stop.
Distinguish get an email, send an email, phone someone, text someone and make a phone call.
Understand vocabulary for mobile phones, text messages and voicemail.
Use polite expressions to start, manage and finish a telephone conversation.
Read telephone numbers aloud, using oh for zero and double for repeated digits.
Talk about communication preferences and how often you go online or use email and phones.
